lessons.title: Physical Real Estate: Rental Yield, Appreciation and Hidden Costs

children.text: Property is India's favourite alternative asset, and most families do not even think of it as alternative. A second flat feels solid, visible and safe in a way a Nifty index fund never does. Chapter 3 gave you three traditional benchmarks: equity, fixed income and gold. Now the same lens goes on the asset most Indian households already hold. What does a flat in Bengaluru or Pune really return once rent, costs and appreciation are added up honestly, and what risks come attached that a brochure never mentions?

body.text: For residential property in Indian cities, rent barely covers the costs of owning it. Almost the entire return comes from price appreciation, which is uncertain, concentrated in one location, and impossible to collect without selling the whole asset.

children.text: The Four Parts of a Property Return
Gross rent.
What the tenant pays you.
Running costs.
Society maintenance, property tax, repairs, empty months and tenant brokerage.
Price appreciation.
The change in what the property would sell for.
Transaction costs.
Stamp duty, registration and brokerage paid once when you buy and again when you sell, which drag down every year's return.

children.text: Rental Yield: Where the Rent Actually Goes

markDefs.definition: Annual rent as a percentage of the property's value, before any costs. A ₹1 crore flat renting for ₹25,000 a month has a gross yield of 3%.
Annual rent minus the owner's running costs, such as maintenance, property tax, repairs and vacancy, as a percentage of the property's value.

children.text: Residential flats in large Indian cities typically have a
gross rental yield
of about 2 to 3.5%. That is already below a bank FD. What reaches you, the
net rental yield

body.caption: Where a year's rent goes: ₹1 crore flat in Bengaluru renting at ₹25,000 a month (illustrative)

cells: Vacancy, about one month a year

children.text: A 3% gross yield became 1.72% before tax. Rental income is also taxable at your slab rate, after a standard 30% deduction on the rent net of municipal taxes, so a landlord in a high bracket keeps closer to 1%. For comparison, a G-Sec pays around 6 to 7% with no tenant, no repairs and no vacancy.

body.title: Calculate a net rental yield
body.prompt: A ₹90 lakh flat in Pune rents for ₹22,500 a month. The owner's annual running costs for maintenance, property tax, repairs and vacancy total ₹90,000. What is the net rental yield, in percent, before income tax?
body.explanation: Gross rent is ₹22,500 × 12 = ₹2,70,000, a 3% gross yield. Net rent is ₹2,70,000 − ₹90,000 = ₹1,80,000. ₹1,80,000 ÷ ₹90,00,000 = 2.0%. One-third of the rent went to costs before the taxman took a share.

children.text: Appreciation: The Real Driver and the Real Uncertainty

With net rent near 1 to 2%, a property's return lives or dies on price growth. Nationally, RBI's house price index has risen at a mid-single-digit pace over the last decade. That national number hides enormous variation. Many parts of NCR and Mumbai saw prices stagnate for years between roughly 2014 and 2020, while some well-connected micro-markets in Bengaluru and Hyderabad did far better. Your flat does not earn the national average. It earns whatever happens to one building, in one locality, in one city.

To see how much appreciation matters, take the Bengaluru flat over 10 years. Assume ₹7 lakh of stamp duty, registration and brokerage on purchase (₹1.07 crore in total), 1% brokerage on sale, and rent and costs both growing 5% a year. Change only the appreciation rate.

body.text: At 5% appreciation, the flat returns less than a government bond, with far more risk and effort. It needs about 8% appreciation, year after year for a decade, just to earn a modest premium over fixed income. That is the hurdle every residential investment has to clear before leverage and tax.

body.title: Ready flat vs under-construction: two different risk profiles

children.text: An under-construction flat is often cheaper, sometimes by 10 to 20%, and that discount is effectively a premium for taking on the developer's risk. The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 requires developers to register projects and keep 70% of buyers' money in a separate account for that project, which has reduced diversion of funds. It has not removed the risk of delays or a developer running into financial trouble.

children.text: The EMI Reality Check

Because the rent on an Indian flat is so low relative to its price, an investment flat bought with a loan almost never pays for itself. The gap between EMI and rent comes out of your salary every month for years. Use the calculator to check: try an ₹80 lakh loan at 8% for 20 years, then compare the EMI with a rent of ₹25,000 a month.

body.title: What drives the return?
body.question: For a typical rented flat in a large Indian city, which component usually contributes most to the investor's total return over 10 years?
options: The security deposit collected from the tenant
body.explanation: With net yields of around 1.5 to 2.5%, rent is a small part of the return. Appreciation drives most of it, and in the illustration it swings the 10-year return from about 1.3% to 8.6% a year.

body.title: Indian property terms
body.textWithBlank: The minimum property value set by a state government for calculating stamp duty is commonly called the ___ rate.
body.explanation: It is called the circle rate in Delhi and much of North India, the ready reckoner rate in Maharashtra, and the guidance or guideline value in states such as Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Stamp duty is charged on the higher of this value and the actual deal price.

body.title: Anita's second flat
body.scenario: Anita, 42, lives in her own flat in Gurugram and has ₹40 lakh in savings. She wants to buy a second flat for ₹1.2 crore as an investment. The plan: ₹30 lakh down payment, about ₹8 lakh in stamp duty, registration and brokerage, and a ₹90 lakh home loan at 8% for 20 years, with an EMI of about ₹75,300. The flat would rent for around ₹30,000 a month. Her builder friend says: "Gurugram always goes up. Rent covers part of the EMI, and in ten years you will double your money."
body.prompt: Assess this plan using the ideas from this lesson and Chapter 2.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Cash flow: the EMI of about ₹75,300 is more than double the ₹30,000 rent, before maintenance, property tax and vacancy. Anita would fund a gap of about ₹45,000 or more every month from her salary.

2. Liquidity: ₹38 lakh of her ₹40 lakh savings would go in on day one, leaving almost no emergency fund. Liquidity risk would be extreme.

3. Yield: ₹30,000 × 12 = ₹3.6 lakh, a 3% gross yield. After costs, the net yield is closer to 2%, well below her 8% loan rate.

4. Leverage: her equity is small relative to the flat. As Chapter 2 showed, a 10% price fall could wipe out a large part of her down payment, while interest keeps running.

5. "Always goes up" and "double in ten years": doubling needs about 7.2% appreciation a year, before costs. Parts of NCR saw years of flat prices between roughly 2014 and 2020, so this is a hope, not a plan.

6. Concentration: she would have two flats in the same city, so her home and her main investment would share the same local risks.

A sounder approach: keep an emergency fund, compare the expected return with the hurdle from this lesson (roughly 8% appreciation just to beat fixed income modestly), and consider whether diversified, liquid investments would meet her goals with far less risk.

points: A property's return has four parts: gross rent, running costs, price appreciation and transaction costs, before tax and leverage.
Metro residential gross yields of about 2 to 3.5% shrink to roughly 1.5 to 2.5% net, and closer to 1% after tax for high-bracket landlords.
Appreciation drives almost everything: the illustrative Bengaluru flat returned 1.3% a year at 0% growth and 8.6% at 8% growth.
At 5% appreciation, a rented flat can earn less than a government bond, with far more risk and effort.
Physical property scores high on liquidity, valuation, leverage and concentration risk, plus developer, title, tenant and policy risks.
With EMIs far above rent, a leveraged investment flat is usually funded by your salary, not by its tenant.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any property. Yields, costs, appreciation rates and returns are illustrative and vary widely by city, locality and property. Stamp duty, GST and tax rules vary by state and change over time. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser, a tax professional and a property lawyer before making decisions.
